script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, this is the rock pool project. How did the fieldwork go in the end?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Mostly well, I think. We managed to survey both shores, the sheltered bay at Kelso and the exposed headland at Point Morran, and we did twenty quadrats at each.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Though it wasn't exactly smooth. Our second visit to the headland had to be called off completely. There was a storm warning, and the coastguard advised people to stay off the rocks, so we lost almost a week.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: And the other big headache was the seaweeds. We were fine with the obvious ones, the wracks and the kelp, but there were several small red seaweeds that we just couldn't put a name to, even with the field guide.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: That's very common. What did you do with them?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We photographed them and recorded them as 'red algae, unidentified', so at least they're in the counts.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Sensible. And no problems with equipment?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Well, we nearly lost a quadrat. A wave picked it up, but I managed to grab it before it went in. And the camera battery died on the first morning, but luckily Priya had brought a spare, so that didn't cost us anything.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: I'd half expected the tide times to be a problem too. I'd downloaded a new app and I didn't really trust it, but it turned out to be completely accurate.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Good. So, results. Was there anything you didn't expect?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Yes, one thing really surprised us. We predicted that limpets would be more common in the sheltered bay, because there's less wave action to knock them off. But in fact the density of limpets at the exposed site was much higher, nearly double.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: The barnacles were about what we expected, and we hardly saw any crabs at either site, so nothing to compare there.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Interesting. And how are you planning to deal with the limpet result in your discussion?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Well, we wondered about going back to collect more data, to check it wasn't a fluke.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: I wouldn't, honestly. You haven't got time before the deadline, and the weather's unpredictable. And you could look at published studies, but the literature on limpets and exposure is quite mixed, so it won't settle anything. I think the most valuable thing is to be upfront about the limitations of your sampling method. You placed your quadrats at only one height on the shore, didn't you?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Yes, just the mid-shore.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Then explain how that might have produced the result. That shows real scientific thinking, and examiners like that.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Okay, that makes sense.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: And how are you presenting the species counts?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We started doing a bar chart for every species, but there are twenty-three species, so it got ridiculous.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We've now decided to put all the counts into one table, with the two sites side by side. It's much easier to compare at a glance.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Good decision. Now, I've read through your draft, so let me go through it section by section. The introduction is generally accurate, but it goes on for three pages. You've included a lot of general background about oceans that isn't really needed, so it's simply too long. Aim for one page.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Okay, we'll cut it right down.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Your description of the two sites is clear, but it's very hard to picture where your transects were. I'd like to see a diagram of each site, showing the shoreline and where you laid each line.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We could draw that from our field notes.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Then the methods. Now, the basic idea is fine, but someone reading this couldn't repeat your study. How big were the quadrats? How did you choose where to put them? You need to add a lot more detail there.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Right, we sort of assumed people would know.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: Never assume that. Now, the raw data. You've put all twenty pages of tally sheets in the middle of the report. They're useful evidence, but they break up the flow, so they should go in an appendix at the end.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Fine, that's easy.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: And finally your reference list. The sources themselves are good, but you've used a mixture of styles. The department requires the author-date system, so you'll need to change them all to match that.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Oh, I didn't realise there was a set system.

script.speaker: Dr Hale
script.text: It's in the handbook. Oh, and I should say the discussion section is very well organised. I made a note that I thought there was a factual error in your introduction about tidal ranges, but when I checked, you were right, so ignore that.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: That's a relief. Thanks, Dr Hale.

options.text: It had more limpets than the sheltered shore.
It had fewer crabs than the sheltered shore.
Its barnacles were larger than expected.

questions.explanation: They predicted more limpets in the sheltered bay, but the exposed site had nearly double. Barnacles were as expected and crabs were rare at both sites.

comparing it with published research.
discussing weaknesses in how they sampled.

in a single table comparing both sites
on a map of each site
